full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: This appeal, by leave, by the complainant appellant is from an order dated 14 November, 1995 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division summarily rejecting the revisional application, Criminal Revision No. 1335 of 1995, filed by the appellant under section 10(1A) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 (Act No. XL of 1958), briefly, the Act. 

 4. It was submitted before the High Court Division that (1) the learned Special Judge acted illegally in not addressing the Government immediately on receipt of the complaint as to sanction as required under section 6(5) of the Act and (2) that the order for holding inquiry by the ASP was illegal and improper as his superior/higher officers were made accused in the complaint petition. 

 8. Mr. MA Wahhab Miah, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, while reiterating his submission that the learned Special Judge acted illegally in not addressing the Government by letter immediately on receipt of the complaint which was not accompanied by any sanction as required under the proviso to section 6(5) of the Act, referred to a number of decisions in support of his contention. The learned Advocate submitted that before taking cognisance the learned Special Judge was, first of all, required to comply with the proviso as aforesaid. That having not been done the proceeding was void ab initio. 

 4. Jurisdiction of Special Judges and cognisance of cases by them-(1) A Special Judge shall have jurisdiction within such territorial limits as may be fixed by the "Government" by notification in the official Gazette and any take cognisance of any offence committed or deemed to have been committed within such limits and triable under this Act upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence or upon a report in writing of such facts made by any Police Officer. 

 6 (5)-Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, or in any other law, previous sanction of the Government shall be required for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence under this Act and such sanction shall be sufficient for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence triable under this Act. 

 Provided that in case where the complaint or report referred to in sub-section (1) of section 4 is not accompanied by such sanction the Special Judge shall, immediately on receipt of the complaint or report, address, by letter, the Government in the matter, and if the required sanction is neither received nor refused within sixty days of the receipt of the letter by the Government, such sanction shall be deemed to have been duly accorded. 

 The pre-condition is the obligation on the pare of Special Judge for writing to the Government for sanction. Without doing so, he cannot take cognisance of the case. In such view of the matter, the proceeding was quashed. 

 13. In Ainuddin vs. State PLD 1962 (WP) Karachi 738, the learned Special Judge on the basis of a private complaint held preliminary inquiries against the accused under section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure examining witnesses and then found that the allegation against two of the accused were false and there was prima facie case against one and accordingly, approached the appropriate authorities for according sanction for his prosecution. The complainant moved the High Court in revision against the said order of the learned Special Judge. The learned Single Judge upon noticing the proviso to section 6(5) observed that it is not open to the Special Judge to proceed in the matter unless and until previous sanction is obtained from the appropriate government for the prosecution of such public servant. Under the proviso the learned Special Judge is not empowered impliedly to hold an enquiry whatsoever for finding out a prima facie case against such public servant nor is he competent to decide the question against whom he should seek sanction and against whom he should not seek sanction. The learned Judge further observed that the scheme of the Act limits the jurisdiction of the Special Judge in this respect. The only step he can take on receiving the complaint or the police report is to immediately write to the appropriate Government for obtaining sanction to prosecute the public servant concerned. The question whether the public servant concerned should be prosecuted or not in entirely and completely within the jurisdiction of the appropriate Government. The Special Judge has no say in the matter. It is not for him to decide whether e prima facie case has been made out against the public servant or not. 

 14. Murshed J., as his Lordship then was, sitting in a Division Bench, said the same thing in Chikoni Bewa vs. Abdul Awal PLR (1964) 14 (Dacca) Dacca Series 557 where the learned Senior Special Judge summarily dismissed the petition of complaint considering the same to be unworthy of credit, It was held, referring to the aforesaid provision of law, that the learned Special Judge was bound to forward the petition of complaint to the Provincial Government, and, if he heard nothing from such Government for a period of sixty days, he should have proceeded to trial on the presumption that sanction was accorded by the said Government. 

 15. The learned Additional Attorney-General, who appeared to support the impugned order, submitted that the learned Special Judge is authorised under section 5(6) of the Act to order an investigation by any Police Officer in any case and, as such, he did not commit any illegality by calling for a report from the ASP upon making enquiry. As regards sanction he submitted that since a prosecution begins with the framing of charge, it was enough if the Special Judge received the sanction before actually framing the charge and he having initially called for a police report, the time for writing to the Government for sanction was yet there. In the facts of the case, not writing to the Government immediately on receipt of the complaint as per the proviso was not an illegality, he submitted. In support of his submission that a sanction was sufficient for prosecution under section 6(5) if received before framing of charge and is not a pre-condition for taking cognisance, he referred to Bangladesh vs. Abdur Rahim 35 DLR 249 in which a Division Bench took the view that the Special Judge is required to write to the Government for sanction if on the date of receipt of the complaint or report the sanction is not available, yet the first proviso to section 6(5) of the Act will be substantially complied with if the sanction to prosecute is accorded by the Government before the charge is framed, even if the Special Judge has failed to write to the appropriate authority for necessary sanction, and has taken cognisance of the case without writing to the Government for sanction. 

 "The ratio decidendi of the cases reported in 9 DLR (Dacca) 109 and 10 DLR (Dacca) 321 and 370 is that when a complaint or report against a public servant is not accompanied by a sanction to prosecute a public servant, the Special Judge shall stay his hands if he takes any steps which can in law be interpreted as taking cognizance of the case, the entire prosecution will be void ab initio. The first proviso to section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 has, in our opinion, effected a qualitative change in the position of law. If the complaint or report is not accompanied by a sanction the Special Judge is required to write to the Government immediately for such sanction. To write to the Government for such sanction is, in our opinion, to take cognisance of the case or at least to take a proceeding in connection with the prosecution of the case. As such we think that those decisions which debar the Special Judge from taking cognisance at all without the previous sanction of the Government have lost their validity and relevance owing to the introduction of the first proviso to section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958." 

 18. It is not necessary to make any pronouncement upon the views expressed as above, in view of the decision of this Division referred to above 35 DLR (AD) 324. It will be seen in an appropriate case which of the decisions on the point has or have lost validity. For the present we find no contrary opinion to the requirement of complying with the proviso to section 6(5) if any petition of complaint is not accompanied by sanction as in the present case. The imperative language of the proviso, "the Special Judge shall, immediately on receipt of the complaint", leaves no manner of doubt that before any step is taken the Special Judge has to address the Government in case of sanction not being accompanied with a petition of complaint. 

 19. It is true that In a case under the Act a Special Judge may where he deems it necessary, order an Investigation by any police officer In whose jurisdiction the offence was wholly or partly committed. This step also, however, cannot be taken without complying with the proviso to section 6(5), one of the reasons being that the Government may not give any sanction to prosecute at all. In the present case it cannot be said that the learned Special Judge has acted with sound discretion in asking the ASP to hold an enquiry when admittedly officers much above sound have been made accused in the case. The learned Additional Attorney-General submitted that since the Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police were already transferred from Dinajpur there was no reason to apprehend that the ASP would not be able to hold an influence-free enquiry. It is difficult to accept the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General, for, it is not necessary to be personally present to influence an enquiry by a subordinate junior officer. The question is not of distance but of being above. There are authorities which have found it improper for an enquiry to be held against a person by a person belonging to the same department (29 CrlJ 1928, 958).
